summary: This document specifies using TLS 1.3 to secure the connection between a TACACS+ client and server. TACACS+ is a protocol for authentication, authorization and accounting on network devices, and its original design had weak protection of its traffic. It updates RFC 8907.

plainLanguage.summary: TACACS+ checks who can log into network equipment. Wrapping it in TLS puts its messages in a sealed envelope so spies cannot read them.

questions: which port does tacacs+ over tls use
subtitle: Putting TACACS+ inside a TLS 1.3 connection so device-admin traffic is really encrypted.

tldr.problem: TACACS+ protects its packet bodies only with a weak obfuscation scheme built on MD5, which cannot give real confidentiality, integrity or peer authentication.
tldr.mechanism: TACACS+ runs inside a TLS 1.3 connection on new TCP port 300, with mandatory mutual authentication, and the old obfuscation is dropped.
tldr.outcome: This updates RFC 8907 and obsoletes obfuscation when TLS is used. TLS servers must not accept non-TLS connections, and clients must not fall back to them.

today: RFC 9887 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2025 that updates RFC 8907. It has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: The Problem with TACACS+ Obfuscation
sections.content:
TACACS+ (RFC 8907) gives routers, network access servers and other devices centralized authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA). Its content is highly sensitive, yet the protocol lacks effective confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the connection between server and client. The RFC calls the mechanisms in Section 4.5 of RFC 8907 extremely weak.

The obfuscation is an algorithm the original RFC deliberately does not call encryption. It rests on MD5, which has been shown to be insecure when used for encryption, and this prevents TACACS+ from being used in a deployment compliant with FIPS 140-3. This document updates RFC 8907 to use TLS 1.3 for encryption and authentication, and obsoletes obfuscation.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of hiding TACACS+ messages was like writing in a secret code that is easy to crack. TLS is a real lock.

sections.title: Running TACACS+ over a TLS Connection
sections.content:
TACACS+ over TLS keeps the protocol of RFC 8907, removes obfuscation, and carries everything over TLS 1.3. Peers MUST apply mutual authentication and encrypt all data exchanged. The client makes a TCP connection to the server and MUST immediately begin the TLS handshake, before sending any TACACS+ data. Options that upgrade an initial non-TLS connection MUST NOT be used.

A minimum of TLS 1.3 MUST be used, and earlier versions MUST NOT. Once TLS is up, all TACACS+ messages are sent as TLS application data under the procedures of RFC 8907.

Servers MUST listen on a TCP port distinct from non-TLS servers, and the RFC assigns the well-known port 300. Deployments MAY use another port. Without Single Connection Mode the TCP session is closed when the TACACS+ session completes. Connections in Single Connection Mode MAY last longer but are typically closed after brief inactivity.
sections.plainLanguage: First the two sides shake hands and check each other's ID cards. Only after that do they start talking, and everything they say goes through a sealed tube.

sections.title: How Peers Prove Who They Are
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support certificate-based mutual authentication. Each peer MUST validate the other's certificate path, including revocation checking, per Section 6 of RFC 5280. Where a peer is isolated from the remote peer's CA, implementations MUST support certificate chains stored locally, and the TLS Cached Information Extension SHOULD be implemented. A peer MUST NOT permit connection by any peer presenting an invalid certificate, unless disabled by configuration.

Clients validate server identity following RFC 9525, using DNS-ID, IP-ID or SRV-ID, but not URI-ID. Wildcards are allowed only under the RFC 9525 guidelines and SHOULD be confined to a subdomain dedicated to TACACS+ servers. Servers MUST be able to identify clients either by network address or by a shared identity in the certificate subjectAltName. Implementations MUST support the SNI extension, and clients MUST be able to configure the server name to send.

Implementations MUST support the TLS 1.3 mandatory cipher suites, and the suites offered or accepted SHOULD be configurable.

Implementations MAY also support external pre-shared keys (PSKs) and raw public keys. For PSKs, lengths and identities of at least 16 octets MUST be supported, and PSKs MUST NOT be the same as the shared secrets used for obfuscation.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides show a badge, and each checks the other's badge is real and not cancelled. A shared secret password is allowed as a backup, but it must be a new one.

sections.title: Resumption and the Obfuscation Flag
sections.content:
TLS resumption cuts round trips. A client holding a valid unused ticket from a NewSessionTicket message SHOULD use it, since each ticket is single use. The server SHOULD allow resumption if the ticket has not expired or been used, but MAY require a full handshake. Certificates must be checked for revocation since the last ticket, and the ticket lifetime SHOULD be configurable, including zero seconds. Reuse of a ticket lets passive observers correlate connections, so clients and servers SHOULD follow the tracking preventions of RFC 8446.

For obfuscation, a client opening a TLS connection MUST set the TAC_PLUS_UNENCRYPTED_FLAG bit on every packet to assert that obfuscation is not used. A TLS server receiving a packet without the bit set MUST return an error status with the flag set to 1 and terminate the session. A client receiving such a packet MUST terminate the session and SHOULD log the error.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have visited before, a stamped ticket lets you skip some of the checks. Every message also carries a sticker saying the old secret code is not in use.

sections.title: Avoiding Downgrade and Replay
sections.content:
Adding TLS does not by itself protect servers and clients, so operators and vendors must follow current best practice, including BCP 195. The document changes nothing in core TACACS+ other than deprecating obfuscation, and further documents are planned on password-based authentication.

New production deployments SHOULD use TLS. TLS servers MUST NOT allow non-TLS connections, because of downgrade attacks and misconfiguration, and clients MUST NOT fail back to non-TLS if a TLS connection fails, including during migration. Putting both kinds of server on the same host is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Clients MUST NOT send 0-RTT early data, because of replay risk, and servers MUST abruptly disconnect clients that do. The early_data extension MUST NOT be included. The SNI is sent in cleartext in the client hello, so it can be eavesdropped. Wildcard certificates are a single point of failure if their private key is compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad guy can trick the two sides into using the old unlocked way, the lock is useless. So the rule is simple: no unlocked fallback, ever.

sections.title: Migrating and the Port Number
sections.content:
A new port was chosen over upgrading an existing connection because it makes blocking by port easy, leaves passive intrusion detection of non-TLS traffic unaffected, avoids on-path attacks that interfere with an upgrade, and prevents accidental exposure through misconfiguration. Clients MUST default to port 49 for non-TLS and port 300 for TLS.

During migration, operators may need both TLS and non-TLS servers. That phase is vulnerable to downgrade attacks and should be considered insecure until complete, so the period when any client is configured for both should be minimized. Devices that do not implement TLS need separate non-TLS servers. A YANG model for managing TACACS+ clients, including TLS, is referenced as a separate Internet-Draft.
sections.plainLanguage: The locked door gets its own entrance, so guards can tell at a glance which door a visitor used. While the old door stays open, the building is not fully safe.

sections.title: IANA Port Assignment
sections.content: IANA has allocated the service name tacacss on TCP port 300, described as TLS Secure Login Host Protocol (TACACSS). The assignee is the IESG, the contact is the IETF Chair, and the reference is RFC 9887. The name follows the common practice of appending an s to the name of the non-TLS well-known port. Service discovery is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet's official list now has a line saying port 300 is the locked TACACS+ door.
